title: Minaketana Ramadasa
html:
The Avadhuta's Servant

Listing the branches of Nityananda's tree, Krishnadasa Kaviraja names among them Minaketana Ramadasa:

“Gopala the dancer, Ramabhadra, Gaurangadasa, Nrisimha-chaitanya and Minaketana Ramadasa.” (CC, Adi 11.53)

He tells of him at length in the fifth chapter of the Adi-lila, where he recalls how he himself came to Vrindavana by Nityananda's mercy. The story opens thus:

“Avadhuta Gosani had a servant who was an abode of love; his name was Minaketana Ramadasa.” (CC, Adi 5.161)

In the Bengali he is a bhritya, a servant of the Avadhuta Gosani, and an “abode of prema” (prema-dhama).1 Further on in the same story Kaviraja calls him now Ramadasa, now Minaketana. In the “Bhakti-ratnakara” he is “Sri Minaketana Ramadasa, the charming one,” in the “Narottama-vilasa” “Sri Minaketana Ramadasa Mahashaya.” The biographies also call him Sri Minaketana or simply Ramadasa;2 one of them speaks of him as “a devotee of Nityananda,” another as Nityananda's “dear associate” and “follower.”

Who his parents were, and where and when he appeared in this world, is not known. Nor does anyone say when or where he left this world, and the Vaishnava calendar of Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math has no days for him. Even the place where he lived is not stated exactly: the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” says only that he came to Jhamatpur by invitation, while the biographies suppose that he lived somewhere nearby or in Jhamatpur itself.3

The “Charitamrita” calls Nityananda the Avadhuta — a name for a wanderer bound by no outward rules. His servant was an avadhuta too. In the “Anubhashya” on this verse Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati cites Sridhara Svami's gloss (on the “Bhagavatam,” 3.1.19): an avadhuta is asamskrita-deha, one who takes no care of his body and bears no ritual marks on it. The disciple of the Avadhuta Nityananda, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains, is likewise an eternally perfect maha-bhagavata, a paramahamsa above varnashrama: his body bore the marks of no varna and no ashrama; he was immersed in the mood of Vraja and gave no thought to the body. One of the biographies calls him exactly that — a maha-bhagavata, or paramahamsa — the words with which the “Anubhashya” heads the next verse. Here lies the key to all that happened later in Jhamatpur: Minaketana's actions were neither oddities nor rudeness, but the rapture of a devotee for whom outward rules no longer mattered.

The Other Sankarshana

Who he is in the Lord's eternal pastimes Kavi Karnapura tells. Speaking of Nityananda's associates, he writes:

“The vyuha of Sankarshana, called the One who lies on the Ocean of Milk, became Virachandra, whose form is non-different from Chaitanya; into him, for the sake of the work, entered the brothers Nishatha and Ulmuka. Minaketana Ramadasa is the other Sankarshana, the original vyuha.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 67–68)

Nishatha and Ulmuka are sons of Balarama; according to the verse, they entered Virachandra (Virabhadra), the son of Nityananda, while Minaketana Ramadasa is one person, himself “the other Sankarshana.” This is how Srila Bhaktisiddhanta too reads the verse in the “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 11.53: Nishatha and Ulmuka entered Virachandra for a purpose, and Minaketana Rama is another vyuha of Sankarshana.4 He is one of the intimate associates of Nityananda-Balarama, and so whatever touched his Lord's honour touched him too.

Kirtana in Jhamatpur

Krishnadasa Kaviraja lived at that time in Jhamatpur, a village near Naihati, and in his house the Vaishnavas sang the holy names day and night. He recalls:

“In my house there was sankirtana day and night, and he came there by invitation.” (CC, Adi 5.162)

According to the “Anubhashya,” “day and night” (ahoratra) means eight praharas, a full day and night; pure devotees had the custom of sending letters of invitation to such kirtana festivals. One biography calls this festival an eight-prahara sankirtana; another, a day-long kirtana arranged by Kaviraja himself. When it took place the sources do not say; it is clear only that it was before Kaviraja left for Vrindavana.

“Full of great love, he sat down in the courtyard, and all the Vaishnavas bowed at his feet. As they bowed, he would climb on the back of one, and in his love strike another with his flute or slap yet another.” (CC, Adi 5.163–164)

His appearance and the signs of his love amazed all the guests, and nearly everyone came up to bow to him. And he, forgetful of himself, would climb onto one — onto his shoulders, says one biography — slap another, and strike a third with his flute. The flute in his hand was a cowherd boy's flute: the mood of Vraja in which he was absorbed showed even in his outward form. Those blows were no impertinence, but the play of a maha-bhagavata whom love had raised above all rules of courtesy.

“From those eyes, the very sight of which brings tears to one's heart, flowed an unbroken stream of tears.” (CC, Adi 5.165)

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” adds: one had only to look into his eyes, and tears would rise of themselves.

“At times I saw the hair on some limb stand on end like kadamba blossoms; one limb would stiffen while another trembled. When he roared out ‘Nityananda!’, all who saw it were filled with wonder.” (CC, Adi 5.166–167)

One biography says that all eight sattvika-bhavas, the wondrous signs of divine love, appeared on his body; the “Charitamrita” names among them horripilation, stupor and trembling, as well as tears. Another biography remarks that whenever he uttered Nityananda's name these transformations came over his body, and people marvelled. Intoxicated with prema, he called out “Nityananda!” in a thunderous roar (hunkara), and the hearts of all around opened to divine bliss.

“A Second Romaharshana”

In Kaviraja's house the Deity was served by a brahmana, Gunarnava Mishra:

“A respectable brahmana named Gunarnava Mishra was serving the Deity there.” (CC, Adi 5.168)

He served the Deity (sri-murti) with faith, but had no wish to give due honour to the Lord's devotee. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” calls such a devotee a kanishtha-adhikari, a devotee of the lowest stage: he has faith enough in the Deity, but cannot recognize a Vaishnava and honour him, and so offends his feet. One biography calls Gunarnava the pujari of the house, another a priest (purohita) who performed the puja of the Deity.5

“Ramadasa sat in the courtyard, but the brahmana did not greet him; seeing this, Minaketana said angrily: ‘Here is a second Romaharshana Suta, who did not rise to greet Baladeva when he saw Him!’” (CC, Adi 5.169–170)

Everyone bowed before Ramadasa, while the servant of the Deity did not so much as address him.6 Minaketana understood that this brahmana had no faith in Nityananda and was slighting him precisely as Nityananda's servant — and lost all regard for him. One biography remarks that he spoke the words about Romaharshana to teach the world.

The comparison comes from the “Bhagavatam” (10.78.22–28), as both the “Anubhashya” and the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” point out. In Naimisharanya Romaharshana Suta, a disciple of Vyasa, was reciting the “Bhagavatam” at the sages' request, seated on the vyasasana. When Baladeva arrived, everyone rose to meet Him; only Romaharshana did not come down from his seat or greet Him — and for this Baladeva punished him, taking his life. Gunarnava acted just as unfittingly: to fail to honour Nityananda's servant is to fail to honour Balarama Himself. One biography draws a lesson from this: a proud man is fit neither to speak the “Bhagavatam,” which is non-different from Krishna, nor to serve the Deity.

Can Minaketana be called proud for this anger? Bhaktivinoda Thakura answers: devotees find no fault in him and do not call him proud. It was anger not for himself but for his Lord, the anger of Balarama's servant and friend — and how little worldly resentment there was in it the “Charitamrita” shows at once:

“Having said this, he danced and sang and rejoiced; but the brahmana went on with his service to Krishna and showed no anger.” (CC, Adi 5.171)

The “Anubhashya” heads this verse: even when a Vaishnava is offended, he does not look for faults in others. Nor did the brahmana answer anger with anger: he quietly went on serving Krishna.7

The Broken Flute

The festival ended, and Ramadasa, having blessed everyone, made ready to leave. Then came what Kaviraja goes on to describe:

“At the end of the festival he was leaving, having given his blessings, when a dispute arose between him and my brother. My brother had firm faith in Chaitanya Prabhu, but towards Nityananda only a semblance of faith.” (CC, Adi 5.172–173)

In the Bengali, the brother had towards Nityananda only vishvasa-abhasa, “a semblance of faith”; the “Anubhashya” explains: “very slight faith.” He had seen how the guest behaved, and he started an argument with him; according to one biography, this was after Gunarnava had left. Bhaktivinoda Thakura, introducing this chapter, writes that the brother took the pujari's side and did not acknowledge Nityananda's greatness. The brother's name, according to the “Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” was Shyamadasa.

“Knowing this, Ramadasa was grieved at heart, and so I rebuked my brother: ‘The two brothers are one body, equally manifest. If you do not accept Nityananda, you will be utterly ruined. You have faith in one but show the other no respect: your standard is the logic of half a hen. If you accept neither, you are an atheist; and to accept one and not the other is hypocrisy.’” (CC, Adi 5.174–177)

The brother's unbelief wounded Ramadasa deeply. But Kaviraja took his side and rebuked his brother before the guest had gone;8 according to one biography, he also told his brother that Nityananda is an avatara of Baladeva and that it is wrong to think Him lower than Chaitanya. Faith in Chaitanya without faith in Nityananda is not devotion but hypocrisy; and so one cannot say of the brother that he was a good devotee who lacked only one thing: the Two Brothers are one body.9

“In anger Ramadasa broke his flute and went away, and at that very moment my brother was ruined.” (CC, Adi 5.178)

Breaking the cowherd's flute he had brought to the festival, Minaketana left a house where his Lord was not honoured. According to one biography, he simply left, displeased. The Bengali says of the brother: “at that very moment my brother met with utter ruin” (sarva-nasha). One biography explains that though the brother was devoted to Gaura, the offence against a devotee destroyed him and he fell; another, that he lost all his devotion. Ramadasa did not curse him: he only went away, and the ruin was the fruit of the offence against a Vaishnava and of unbelief in Nityananda.10

Mercy for the Defender

Kaviraja tells this story not to condemn his brother. He sums up:

“Thus I have told of the power of His servant. Now I tell of something more — the nature of His mercy. Because I had rebuked my brother — and He counted this as a virtue — that night the Lord appeared to me. In a village called Jhamatapura, near Naihati, Nityananda-Rama appeared to me in a dream.” (CC, Adi 5.179–181)

Kaviraja had only stood up for Nityananda's servant — and this small thing was enough for the Lord. In the dream Nityananda revealed His form to him, surrounded by His associates in the dress of cowherds, and said:

“‘O Krishnadasa, Krishnadasa, do not be afraid! Go to Vrindavana: there everything can be attained.’ Saying this, He touched me with His hand and sent me forth; and the Lord disappeared with His associates.” (CC, Adi 5.195–196)

So he gained a life in Vrindavana, and, according to one biography, the service of the feet of Radha and Krishna as well. Another biography tells the dream thus: Nityananda with His associates encouraged him and bade him go to Vrindavana for his supreme welfare.

The lesson is twofold. An offence against a devotee ruins even one who is faithful to Gaura; and, conversely, merely defending Nityananda's servant was enough to win His mercy and Vrindavana. One biography concludes that by serving Nityananda's associates one soon obtains His mercy. Kaviraja's story also shows how dear Minaketana is to Nityananda; and such are all His followers: they deliver the most fallen and fulfil every desire.

In Jahnava's Company

Later we see Minaketana Ramadasa in the company of Jahnava-devi, Nityananda's shakti. When a great festival was being prepared in Kheturi, Narottama's birthplace, word came to Khardaha, and Nityananda's associates asked Vasudha and Jahnava for leave to go there. The “Narottama-vilasa” lists them; among them:

“Sri Minaketana Ramadasa Mahashaya, Nakadi, Sri Balarama and others full of prema. All submitted at the feet of the two Ishvaris that they wished to go to Kheturi.” (“Narottama-vilasa” 6.190–191)

Narahari Chakravarti tells in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” how Jahnava set out from Khardaha:11

“With her went the maha-bhagavatas, at the sight of whom the three worlds are purified: Krishnadasa Sarakhela, Madhava Acharya, Raghupati Vaidya Upadhyaya, most noble, Sri Minaketana Ramadasa, the charming one, Murari Chaitanya, Jnanadasa, Mahidhara.” (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 10.372–374)

The words that the mere sight of these Vaishnavas purifies the three worlds are said of the whole company — and so of Ramadasa too. With Jahnava also went Kamalakara Pippalai, Sri Shankara and many others;12 her way lay through Ambika-Kalna, Navadvipa and Shantipur. The “Prema-vilasa” (19.306–311) and the biographies also name Minaketana Ramadasa among those who came with Jahnava from Khardaha.

On the second day of the festival in Kheturi, in the courtyard of the house where Jahnava stayed, he sat down to the meal with her other companions (“Narottama-vilasa” 8.48–50). And when Jahnava set out from Kheturi for Vrindavana, she told him, Vrindavana, Kamalakara Pippalai and a few other Vaishnavas to return to Khardaha:

“Sri Minaketana Ramadasa, Vrindavana, Kamalakara Piplai and some others — to all these the Ishvari gave the command to go to Khardaha; having taken leave, no one could be calm.” (“Narottama-vilasa” 8.152–153)

The same Narahari Chakravarti, in the “Namamrita-samudra,” where his prayers call upon the Lord's associates, turns to him as well:

“O Sri Minaketana Ramadasa, full of prema, grant me joy in the qualities of Nityananda!” (“Namamrita-samudra” 42)

Nothing more is known of him.

Significance

Minaketana Ramadasa is a servant of the Avadhuta Nityananda, an “abode of prema,” one of the branches of His tree, and in the eternal pastimes “the other Sankarshana.” His rapture of love — tears that made everyone around him weep, the thunderous call “Nityananda!”, the blows of his flute that puzzle those who measure a Vaishnava by outward rules — shows what Nityananda's associates are like. His anger at disrespect to Nityananda did not make him proud: devotees do not find fault with him, and he himself at once danced and sang. Through him Krishnadasa Kaviraja received the lesson that began his journey to Vrindavana: the Two Brothers are one body, and to slight Nityananda's servant brings ruin, while to defend him brings His mercy.

Notes

  1. One biography assigns this verse to Adi 5.162; probably a different numbering of the edition.
  2. He should not be confused with his namesakes: Abhirama Thakura, who was also called Ramadasa, one of the twelve gopalas sent with Nityananda to Gauda (CC, Adi 10.116, 11.13); Ramadasa, the son of Shivananda Sena (CC, Adi 10.62); Ramadasa of Phulia, a disciple of Haridasa (“Prema-vilasa” 24); Ramadasa, a branch of Chaitanya's tree (CC, Adi 10.113); and Minaketana, son of Kamai, in a genealogy of kulina brahmanas (“Prema-vilasa” 24.881).
  3. One and the same biography says in one place that, judging by Kaviraja's account, he lived somewhere near Jhamatpur, and in another that he too lived in Jhamatpur. The twentieth-century reference work “Gaudiya-vaishnava- abhidhana” names as his shripatas Jhamatpur and Balapa-grama (Radhanagara) near Rampurhat, where Krishna and Balarama are served and where his samadhi stands.
  4. Some biographies understand the verse differently: as if Nishatha and Ulmuka (in one of them, “Unmukha”) entered an expansion of Nityananda and became two persons, Minaketana and Ramadasa. And since the “Charitamrita” and the “Bhakti-ratnakara” clearly speak of one person, they suppose that both brothers entered the one Minaketana Ramadasa. But according to the Sanskrit (amum, “into him,” that is, into Virachandra of the previous verse), Nishatha and Ulmuka entered Virachandra, and there is no contradiction between the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” and the “Charitamrita.”
  5. One biography says elsewhere that Gunarnava was invited to the festival as a pujari; according to the “Charitamrita,” he served the Deity in Kaviraja's own house.
  6. That Ramadasa sat down in the courtyard the “Charitamrita” says plainly (Adi 5.163). In verse 5.169 (angane vasiya, “sitting in the courtyard,” in the Gaudiya Math edition) these words can also be taken of the brahmana: so the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” understands them (“Gunarnava Mishra, the servant of the Deity, sitting in the courtyard, did not greet Nityananda's servant”), and after it one of the biographies, though elsewhere the same biography seats Ramadasa in the courtyard. We follow verse 5.163.
  7. One and the same biography tells this differently in two places: in one, Gunarnava made no reply to the reproach and went on with his service; in the other, he was even glad that Ramadasa had reproached him. That Ramadasa danced and sang, the biographies do not mention.
  8. According to one biography, Ramadasa, on learning of the brother's unbelief, broke his flute and went away, and only after that did Kaviraja rebuke his brother; in the “Charitamrita” (Adi 5.174–178) and in another biography the rebuke comes before Ramadasa leaves.
  9. One biography quotes verse 5.175 with a misprint (“এক অনু” for “একতনু,” “one body”), followed, in quotation marks as Kaviraja's words, by “to accept one and not the other — this is your godlessness and hypocrisy.” That is not a verse but a paraphrase of verses 5.176–177 after the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya”; from there too, without naming the source, come the reflection on Romaharshana and the remark that devotees do not blame Minaketana.
  10. One biography calls the brother's ruin “the consequence of a curse.” Neither the “Charitamrita” nor the other biographies speak of any curse.
  11. One biography names Narahari Sarakara Thakura as the author of the “Bhakti-ratnakara”; in fact it was written by Narahari Chakravarti (Ghanashyama Dasa), while Narahari Sarakara of Shrikhanda was an associate of Mahaprabhu.
  12. One biography includes Abhirama Thakura in this list as well, but in the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (10.374) he is not there: in that place stands “Sri Minaketana Ramadasa, the charming one.”
